issues.legal_issue: Capital gains on land compulsorily acquired through the ordinary acquisition process accrue when the statutory stage for vesting is reached, even if the beneficiary was already in possession of the land.
material_facts: The beneficiary college remained in possession of leased land after the lease expired, but there was no evidence that the owner had assented to continued possession; the college therefore remained a tenant at sufferance.
The government did not take possession of the land before the award, and the acquisition proceeded through the ordinary process rather than the urgency process.
The award fixed compensation and recorded that interest was payable from the earlier notification date, but that interest award did not vest the land in the government on the notification date.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was completed, and capital gains accrued, when the award was made; the gains were therefore chargeable for the previous year containing that date, not the year containing the notification date.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 45 and 2(47) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, gains from transfer of a capital asset are chargeable in the previous year in which the transfer occurs, and compulsory acquisition is a transfer. Under Sections 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, land acquired through the ordinary process vests in the government after the award and taking of possession; under the urgency process, vesting follows possession taken under that process after the statutory waiting period. A notification alone does not divest the owner or vest the land. Where possession was taken before the statutory stage for vesting, it is related to that stage rather than treated as completing the transfer earlier. The Court relied on Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Godrej and Boyce, Fruit & Vegetable Merchants Union v. Delhi Improvement Trust, Lt. Governor of Himachal Pradesh v. Avinash Sharma, Buddaiah v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, S. Appala Narasamma v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, and Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Pandari Laxmaiah. Sections 108(q), 111(a), and 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and Nand Ram v. Jagdish Prasad informed the Court’s conclusion that continued possession after lease expiry, without the owner’s assent, did not displace the owner’s title.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_case: The case concerns capital gains arising from land transferred through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.ordinary_acquisition_process: The acquisition proceeded through the ordinary process, rather than an urgency process permitting earlier possession and vesting.
predicates.government_did_not_take_possession_befor: The government did not take possession of the land before the award was made.
predicates.beneficiary_remained_in_possession_after: The acquisition beneficiary continued occupying the land after the lease expired.

issues.definition: When land is compulsorily acquired through the ordinary process, the government has not taken possession before the award, and the beneficiary remains in possession after lease expiry, capital gains accrue when the award is made.

issues.legal_issue: An unchallenged tax decision for another assessment year does not prevent the revenue from contesting the timing of capital gains in a materially different acquisition case when it has just cause.
material_facts: An earlier decision for another assessment year concerned a different parcel of land, for which possession was taken on a specified date and the acquisition was treated as urgent.
In the present case, the acquisition followed the ordinary process, and the actual date of government possession had not been established in the earlier proceedings.
The earlier decision was not appealed, but the revenue challenged the decision in the present case, and the Court found that the cases and applicable acquisition processes differed.
issues.conclusion: The earlier unchallenged decision did not preclude the revenue from maintaining that the transfer in this case was completed on the award date.
issues.legal_principle: Berger Paints India Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, relying on Union of India v. Kaumudini Narayan Dalal, Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Narendra Doshi, and Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Shivsagar Estate, establishes that the revenue should not challenge in another case a legal position it has accepted in one case without just cause. That principle does not bar a challenge where the cases are materially different or there is just cause; an earlier decision involving a different acquisition process and established possession facts does not control a later, distinct case.

rule.if: revenue_challenge_in_tax_case and same_taxpayer_had_prior_unappealed_tax_decision and acquisition_processes_differed and material_possession_facts_differed

predicates.revenue_challenge_in_tax_case: The revenue contests the treatment of an issue in a tax case.
predicates.same_taxpayer_had_prior_unappealed_tax_d: The same taxpayer had an unappealed decision on the issue in another assessment case.
predicates.acquisition_processes_differed: The acquisition process in the earlier case differed from the process in the present case.
predicates.material_possession_facts_differed: The facts about possession material to the timing of transfer differed between the cases.

issues.definition: When the revenue contests an issue in a tax case despite an unappealed decision for the same taxpayer, it may do so if the acquisition processes and material possession facts differ.
